title: Reskinned my turn based drone/missile warfare strategy game.
author: Tom_Baron
selftext:
This was a first attempt using claude design to build graphics and im pretty happy with the result as a first pass. Claude design hands off the package and claude code implements.

The city view and attack/defence simulation as above are done. UI and world map need doing next.

But i spent 5 hours last night just iterating over radar mechanics. Claudes initial attempt made fog of war almost irrelevant. I want a mixture of chess and battleships in the attack phase and you can launch attacks in waves, targetting anywhere in an enemy city and dogleg your weapons to potentially bypass airdefences, each type of building has a direct effect on your city. If your factories are damaged you cant build as many missiles or drones. If your launchers are struck, you cant fire a full wave of missilies and strategically if your radars get damaged now, the fog of war starts lifting, firstly to show where your material buildings are but not what they are and if fully destroyed, what they are too. Direct strikes now open up a grid of intelligence on the enemy city too.

I also had to allow for pooling of intelligence between players of each faction. The game is multiplayer split into two sides and im still heavily in the weeds working out how players can plan strategically together to take advantage of the enemy weaknesses!

Needless to say im having a great time building this!

comments.author: AshenThroneDev
comments.body: The radar-damage-lifts-fog idea is great, it turns scouting into something you attack instead of a menu. One thing that kept our fog meaningful in Ashen Throne: the rule is that you can't act on anything you can't see, not just that it's dimmed. The moment a system "helpfully" lets you target a tile you can only half see, fog becomes decoration, which sounds like what happened with the first radar pass. Tying vision to a building you can lose is exactly the right lever, because losing it then changes what you're allowed to do, not just what you can see.
